items.title: HERE mappa l’Italia in 3D: sulle strade i veicoli per censire anche i cartelli e i negozi
items.summary: I veicoli HERE percorreranno le strade in diverse città italiane per raccogliere dati ad alta precisione e creare mappe più realistiche e più dettagliate ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
HERE ha avviato in Italia un nuovo progetto di mappatura tridimensionale ad alta precisione. La società percorrerà alcune aree del territorio nazionale con veicoli dotati di tecnologie avanzate e pensati per acquisire dati stradali estremamente dettagliati e immagini panoramiche a livello stradale.

L’obiettivo è aggiornare e arricchire le mappe digitali del Paese , rendendole più accurate e più adatte alle esigenze della mobilità moderna.

In particolare, la campagna italiana riguarda la raccolta di informazioni utili alla creazione di mappe 3D evolute, capaci di rappresentare con maggiore precisione le strade, la segnaletica e i punti di interesse presenti sul territorio.

Il lavoro che sta già svolgendo HERE punta quindi a raccogliere un insieme molto ricco di informazioni: dalla geometria delle carreggiate alla segnaletica orizzontale e verticale, fino alla presenza di elementi urbani e servizi lungo il percorso.

I veicoli utilizzati per l’acquisizione dei dati sono chiaramente identificabili grazie al logo HERE . Durante il passaggio sulle strade italiane, stanno raccogliendo immagini tridimensionali a livello stradale e dati ad alta precisione.

Tra le informazioni rilevate rientrano anche punti di interesse come esercizi commerciali, stazioni di servizio e ristoranti . Si tratta di elementi importanti perché le mappe digitali oggi devono supportare servizi di navigazione più intelligenti, applicazioni per la logistica, sistemi di assistenza alla guida e soluzioni per la gestione della mobilità urbana.

I veicoli HERE stanno percorrendo le principali arterie stradali del Paese e le vie di alcune città selezionate. L’attività viene svolta senza interferire con il normale flusso del traffico .

Spiegare perché oggigiorno servano mappe dettagliate e di qualità può sembrare superfluo. Tutti, su base quotidiana, fruiamo di sistemi di navigazione, cerchiamo i percorsi più veloci o quelli più comodi, pianifichiamo viaggi e spostamenti con i mezzi pubblici, a piedi, in bici o con le auto.

Il lavoro di HERE però è pensato sia per l’oggi sia, ancora più importante, per il domani.

Perché nel caso dei veicoli a guida autonoma, che saranno sempre più diffusi nei prossimi anni, il ruolo della mappa è ancora più centrale. Le auto dotate di sistemi avanzati di assistenza alla guida hanno bisogno di informazioni precise sull’ambiente stradale : dalle corsie ai limiti di velocità segnalati; dagli incroci ai punti critici fino alle caratteristiche del percorso. Sono questi i loro "occhi" e "orecchie" che usano per muoversi nell'ambiente urbano ed extraurbano. Una mappa ad alta definizione può quindi contribuire a rendere questi sistemi più affidabili e più consapevoli del contesto in cui operano.

In più, mappe dettagliate e aggiornate servono anche alle aziende per ottimizzare i propri beni; alle istituzioni per gestire meglio le infrastrutture urbane; e agli operatori della mobilità per sviluppare servizi più efficienti. Sapere dove si trovano le strade, i servizi, i punti di interesse, i flussi del traffico e le infrastrutture permette di migliorare la pianificazione e di costruire strumenti più utili per i cittadini, le imprese e le pubbliche amministrazioni.

I dati raccolti da HERE in Italia saranno utilizzati per creare mappe dettagliate e ricche di informazioni , progettate proprio per supportare, fra le altre cose, i veicoli ad elevata automazione e i servizi innovativi. Le possibili ricadute riguardano la sicurezza stradale, la riduzione della congestione del traffico e una maggiore efficienza della mobilità urbana.

Ma non solo in Italia. HERE sta acquisendo dati stradali ad alta precisione e raccogliendo immagini panoramiche a livello stradale in diversi Paesi del mondo, per mantenere le proprie mappe sempre più complete e aderenti alla realtà.

Le città cambiano, la viabilità viene modificata, nascono nuovi servizi, vengono introdotte nuove limitazioni e cambiano le abitudini di spostamento: per questo motivo le mappe vanno considerate infrastrutture digitali che devono evolvere insieme al territorio .

Per acquisire le informazioni stradali, HERE sta utilizzando veicoli equipaggiati con tecnologie di ultima generazione. Questi mezzi sono in grado di raccogliere immagini e dati relativi all’ambiente circostante, così da costruire una rappresentazione digitale tridimensionale e dettagliata delle aree percorse.

Una mappa utile ai servizi di nuova generazione deve essere precisa, coerente e aggiornata. Deve permettere di riconoscere gli elementi rilevanti della strada e restituire informazioni affidabili a chi sviluppa applicazioni di navigazione, sistemi di mobilità connessa o soluzioni per flotte e infrastrutture urbane.

Le mappe ad alta precisione possono diventare una base tecnologica per diversi ambiti: dalla guida assistita alla logistica, dalla pianificazione urbana alla gestione del traffico, fino ai servizi digitali basati sulla posizione. È proprio in questa direzione che si muove il progetto di HERE in Italia.

Un aspetto centrale del progetto riguarda la tutela della privacy. Le immagini acquisite vengono inizialmente archiviate a bordo dei veicoli e successivamente trasferite in forma criptata, per poi essere conservate in strutture sicure. Prima della pubblicazione, le immagini vengono elaborate con software avanzati e algoritmi progettati per rilevare e oscurare volti e targhe. La pubblicazione avviene esclusivamente dopo la completa anonimizzazione di questi elementi .

In ogni caso, HERE prevede un'ulteriore procedura di segnalazione per i casi in cui un’immagine non risultasse correttamente oscurata. In questa eventualità, l’utente può accedere all’immagine online e selezionare il link “Segnala immagine”, collocato nell’angolo inferiore sinistro della mappa.

La campagna di mappatura tridimensionale che HERE sta portando avanti in Italia è un lavoro tecnico e spesso poco visibile all’utente finale, ma allo stesso tempo è fondamentale per molti dei servizi che già oggi usiamo quotidianamente e per quelli che diventeranno sempre più diffusi nei prossimi anni.

Dalla navigazione alle auto connesse, dalla logistica alla mobilità urbana, la qualità dei dati geografici è destinata a incidere sempre di più sul modo in cui ci spostiamo e gestiamo le città.

items.title: 'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
items.summary: More than 80 people have been killed in the mob violence, the BBC finds after gathering data from six African nations.
items.content:
More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.

The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.

"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.

His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.

Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.

The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.

They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.

In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.

At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.

"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.

He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.

Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.

Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.

Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.

He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.

On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.

Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.

"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.

In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.

"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.

Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."

This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.

Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."

Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.

The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.

Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.

Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.

"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.

With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.

Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.

Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.

His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.

People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.

Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.

The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.

Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.

The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.

The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.

As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria .

The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.

After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".

"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.

He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.

Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.

Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.

"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.

"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

Attacks on people like me happen every time my country has an election

items.title: Why Nepal floods should worry India
items.summary: The disaster comes as a warning as climate change raises shared Himalayan risks.
items.content:
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders.

India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts.

Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood.

And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side.

Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system.

Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges.

Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border.

A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep.

Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).

India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers.

Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone.

Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala.

Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected.

Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda.

"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD.

Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk.

Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments.

Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels.

How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain.

So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India.

The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood.

"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction.

Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river.

According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained.

"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha.

The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal.

For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream.

Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara.

A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours.

India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts.

They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment.

A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger.

For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time".

A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists.

Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal.

The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate.

But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India.

Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India.

"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal.

Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment.

"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal.

Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream.

The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management.

"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha.

In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine.

Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger".

"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says.

A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path.

That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure.

It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material.

Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts.

High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast.

items.title: Sydney police investigate second possible mistaken identity killing in two days
items.summary: Wednesday's fatal shooting of a man in his 40s comes after a university student was gunned down on Tuesday.
items.content:
Police in Sydney are investigating a second possible mistaken identity killing at the hands of organised crime in less than 48 hours.

About 15:15 local time on Wednesday, emergency services rushed to a home in Merrylands West after reports a man in his 40s had been targeted in a drive-by shooting. He died at the scene.

A day earlier, about 03:40 on Tuesday, a university student in his 20s with no criminal ties, was shot during a home invasion in Glen Alpine in the city's southwest. He also died at the scene.

Police say the Tuesday shooting appears to be an "innocent life" taken by organised crime while Wednesday's fatal attack may have targeted the "wrong person".

Police believe the man had arrived at the Merrylands West home just moments before he was shot in the doorway.

Asked if investigators were treating the case as a suspected mistaken identity, police said: "Tragically, that is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by these offenders".

"The victim has no links that we are aware of to organised crime, however he has associated with people that reside at this address," Det Supt Simon Glasser said on Wednesday.

The residents of the home were "very well known to police" with links to organised crime, but the man who was shot was "quite likely" a business associate, Glasser said.

Earlier, New South Wales Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon had described Tuesday's killing of Marco Tapia, a university student who was only known to police over a traffic offence, as "completely unacceptable".

"The fact that what appears to be an innocent life was taken [on Tuesday] is something that no community should accept and no community should live in fear of violence," Lanyon said.

"I don't want any innocent member of the community to be impacted by organised crime. We will not tolerate it."

Shortly after Tuesday's fatal shooting, a known organised crime figure posted in a message on social media: "popped the wrong person, didn't even get the right house".

Earlier this year, a Sydney grandfather was allegedly kidnapped and murdered in what police believe was a case of mistaken identity.

Chris Baghsarian, 85, was taken from his home in a pre-dawn raid and his body was found two weeks later near a golf course. Several people have been arrested and charged in the matter.

And last year a Sydney plumber was shot dead in front of his family home in what police said was also a case of mistaken identity.

items.title: Who is Alejandro Betancourt, colourful oil baron behind US-Venezuela oil deal?
items.summary: The 46-year-old figure of international intrigue has an apparent knack for being in the right place at the right time.
items.content:
President Donald Trump has called the deal granting the US control of strategic Venezuelan oil fields "the biggest in history".

North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep), a company little known outside the South American country, will oversee the production and sale of 17 oil fields containing about 65bn barrels of crude.

And at the heart of it is Alejandro Betancourt López, the Venezuelan oil baron who heads the Barbados-registered firm.

The 46-year-old has a history of doing business with the Venezuelan government since the time of the late President Hugo Chávez.

But he has also found himself under investigation in five different countries. He has previously denied wrongdoing and has never been convicted of a crime.

So who is the fixer picked to deliver on Trump's oil abundance plan?

Leopoldo Alejandro Betancourt López was born in the Venezuelan capital of Caracas in February 1980 into a middle-class family.

A graduate of Suffolk University in Boston, Massachusetts, he is estimated to be worth around $2.6bn (£1.9bn).

Although his CV attributes his success to his "entrepreneurial spirit", Venezuelan journalists who have followed his career maintain that it all began with the connections he made in the classrooms of the Instituto Cumbres de Caracas, a private religious school in the Venezuelan capital.

Venezuelan journalist Alek Boyd, who has been tracking Betancourt since 2011, said that the businessman became a close school friend of Javier Alvarado Pardi, the son of the man who would later become president of Electricidad de Caracas, vice-minister of energy, and an executive at Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) – the state-run oil company.

"In 2009, at the height of the electricity crisis, Alvarado introduced Betancourt and his partners to his father and assured him they could solve the problem… despite having no experience in the electricity sector," said Boyd.

Around that time, Derwick Associates, the engineering firm that Betancourt founded with a cousin, received 12 government contracts, awarded without bidding, for a total of $5bn.

Shortly afterwards, he and other young entrepreneurs doing business with the Venezuelan government were nicknamed "bolichicos", a slang term combining the words Bolivarian – referring to Chavez's socialist revolution - and chico, meaning boy.

"It's a term coined by the media, used to describe a group of young people whose only commonality is their success," Jon Sale, the businessman's lawyer in the US, told BBC News Mundo.

Derwick Associates claimed to have completed all of its electrification projects.

But anti-corruption organisations such as Transparency Venezuela and the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project allege that several projects were either not finished or were carried out incorrectly.

A 2018 report by Transparency Venezuela estimated that 11 of the projects awarded to Derwick should have cost $2.1bn. If accurate, this would mean the government would have overpaid by 138%.

Betancourt's legal team has previously rejected the accusations of overbilling as politically motivated attempted smears.

Despite criticism, Venezuelan authorities soon allowed Derwick to venture into the oil industry.

But Betancourt's business activities have not been limited exclusively to Venezuela.

In the mid-2010s, he began his international expansion by acquiring a stake in the Spanish sunglasses company Hawkers, becoming its majority shareholder and president in 2016.

He also acquired banking entities in Switzerland and Africa.

Today, Betancourt's business network encompasses some 50 companies distributed across 16 countries, according to investigations by Transparency Venezuela.

In 2013, the former US ambassador to Venezuela, Otto Reich, filed a lawsuit in an American court against Betancourt and two of his associates for "paying large sums to [Venezuelan] public officials in exchange for awarding them contracts".

The diplomat's lawsuit was dismissed five years later, but the businessman's legal troubles did not disappear.

In recent years, judicial authorities in Spain, Switzerland, Andorra and the US have opened investigations against Betancourt and other "bolichicos" for their alleged involvement in various corruption schemes related to PDVSA.

In 2025, the businessman again made headlines when he was detained twice by British police in London, where he had settled in recent years.

A few days later, Spanish authorities raided Alamín Castle, a palatial estate that Betancourt owned in the province of Toledo.

Both swoops were reportedly linked to an investigation into alleged money laundering initiated by the Swiss public prosecutor's office.

Regarding these allegations, Betancourt's lawyer suggested he was being targeted because of his associations with the other young, brash Venezuelan businessmen.

"This is a group of very successful young entrepreneurs... some have broken the law and others haven't, but they've all been lumped together," Sale, the attorney, told BBC News Mundo.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in an interview with Venezuelan journalist Sergio Novelli, gave three reasons.

"He has a track record of being able to produce oil," he stated first.

Some experts claim that Nabep currently produces around 180,000 barrels of crude per day, just behind Chevron's more than 200,000.

Rubio went on to point out that Betancourt was not currently being investigated by the US.

Finally, Rubio offered a third reason: "He is an individual who strongly supported the opposition."

Unlike others who prospered economically under Chávez, Betancourt and his associates didn't seem to identify ideologically with the late president's movement.

"They simply saw a business opportunity and took advantage of it," Batiz said.

And when the winds shifted, Betancourt shifted with them, forging a relationship with opposition leader Juan Guaidó, during Trump's first term.

That connection helped him make inroads with US officials like Mauricio Claver-Carone, the former US Special Envoy for Latin America, and other figures close to Trump, such as former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, according to Boyd, the Venezuelan journalist.

But when he was involved in a failed attempt to oust Nicolás Maduro in 2019, the then-Venezuelan president retaliated against him, removing him from the oil business and forcing him to live between Madrid and London.

The contacts Betancourt established with the US were reportedly crucial in easing the legal pressure against him in late 2025.

According to the Washington Post, US authorities urged Switzerland to drop its extradition request against the businessman before the British courts.

The request was granted by the Swiss authorities, and last May a London court lifted the travel ban placed upon him.

"Switzerland did not present the evidence requested by the English judges to support its extradition request, and therefore the travel ban was lifted," Betancourt's lawyer told BBC News Mundo, while acknowledging this does not necessarily mean the end of the Swiss investigations.

According to Axios, in the first minutes after the military operation on 3 January that concluded with US forces seizing Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, Betancourt spoke with then-Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez and convinced her to speak with Rubio.

"He acted as an intermediary," said Sale. "He had nothing to do with Maduro's departure, but since he had everyone's trust, he became an intermediary."

On Wednesday, Delcy Rodríguez, now interim president of Venezuela, defended Betancourt, saying he has no pending cases in that country or the US.

"Often a person is judged in the media before in the courts," she said in the oil baron's defence.

For those who have followed Betancourt's career for years, one thing is clear.

"He always manages to be where he needs to be to avoid problems and make money."

items.title: Rocky Horror star Tim Curry's cause of death revealed as coronary artery disease
items.summary: The British actor had significant conditions, cited on his death certificate in Los Angeles County.
items.content:
British actor Tim Curry died of coronary artery disease, his spokesman has confirmed to the BBC.

The Rocky Horror Picture Show star died in his Los Angeles home on 25 August, aged 80.

In addition to the heart condition, Curry had a history of stroke and kidney cancer, which were significant conditions that contributed to his death, his spokesman said, citing a death certificate filed in Los Angeles County.

Stars of stage and screen paid tribute to the actor, who shot to fame as the lingerie-clad Dr Frank-N-Furter in the cult 1975 film The Rocky Horror Picture Show.

After having a near-fatal stroke in 2012, Curry used a wheelchair. He shifted his focus to voice acting exclusively, expressing gratitude that the stroke resulted in paralysis rather than taking away his ability to speak.

He continued to appear at film conventions and published his memoir, Vagabond, last year in which he opened up about the medical incident and his prolonged recovery.

"If there was anything impressed upon me in the aftermath, it was just how remarkable it was that I was still alive," Curry said, according to People , external magazine.

Susan Sarandon leads tributes to Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Tim Curry

'There will only be one Tim Curry' says Rocky Horror star Luke Evans

In a tribute last week, Michael McKean, Curry's co-star in the 1985 comedy whodunit Clue, said that the ailing actor had been in a "grim physical state".

"Even wheelchair bound, he continued to be so sweet and generous with his fans," wrote his Rocky Horror co-star Susan Sarandon, who described Curry as a "funny, sexy, original".

Born in the north-western English town of Warrington in 1946, Curry landed his first acting job after university, appearing in the 1968 London production of the rock musical Hair.

His castmate Richard O'Brien asked him to audition for his new musical, The Rocky Horror Show, the iconic 1973 role in which Curry uttered the line "don't dream it, be it".

His on-screen roles include playing the sadistic clown Pennywise in the 1990 TV version of Stephen King's It, King Arthur in the stage production of Spamalot, Rooster in the 1982 musical film Annie and appearances in Home Alone 2, The Hunt For Red October and Scary Movie 2.

items.title: Stingy bosses and spare change: How much should you give to the office whip-round?
items.summary: Office whip-rounds are a staple of working life but they can raise a lot of awkward questions.
items.content:
Love them, hate them or barely know them, it's a colleague's birthday, wedding or leaving do and there's a collection to mark the occasion.

So how much should you give? And if you're the person organising the collection, how do you chase without feeling like a loan shark or exposing unspoken team dynamics?

The politics of the office whip-round are so sensitive that everyone the BBC spoke to asked us not to use their real name.

For those on a tight budget, the rule is simple: only give to colleagues you've worked with directly.

Lucy, a senior therapist in healthcare, says: "If we haven't worked together, my purse is staying shut."

There's a blunter unspoken truth beneath the surface. "It also depends on if I like you," she admits.

"One colleague's whole demeanor annoyed me, so when she moved roles, I wanted to celebrate with my own drink - not give her money."

Former music journalist Layla is similar, only contributing if she "really likes" the person.

Yet she often avoids office collections on principle, not personality, disliking how impersonal they can feel.

"I'd rather buy my own gift for someone I care about. I hate having to be forced to contribute to a joint collection out of some rubbish sense of obligation," she says.

The decision to give also comes with a question of how much.

Barker has a decade's worth of experience organising and contributing to various collections at a large multi-national company, where he works in research and production.

He says it's normally the same half a dozen people that contribute generously, irrespective of the person or the occasion.

The average a worker gave to a collection was £11.65 in the first three months of the year, according to analysis of over 5,000 contributions by website GiftRound.

Junior workers can often face the biggest dilemma. Felicity, now mid-career, remembers one horror story from her first job as a teenager.

Working at a car garage aged 17, she was suddenly thrust an envelope to give money for a mechanic who was retiring. The team was small and tight-knit, so everyone was expected to contribute.

"Not only did I not really know anyone at that stage, but I also had no money to give - I was still living at home and being paid hardly anything.

"As it was after lunch, I'd used my notes. In a panic I threw in all the spare change I had left, basically a load of coppers."

She says: "I thought I'd got away with it until the person collecting shouted 'who on earth put in all this change'. Everyone laughed and I couldn't ever admit it was me."

Today, Felicity usually gives between £5 and £10 but goes up to £20 for a close work friend or long-time colleague.

Barker says it tends to be rank-and-file workers who contribute most often.

"Surprisingly – to me – they're not some of the best paid people in the department," he explains. "Often those in senior positions don't give".

Those on big wages not paying their way may seem stingy. But the reality from the top can look very different, as former senior civil service veteran Darren explains.

In a leadership position managing over 200 people, many of them contractors, office collections were common as staff churn was frequent.

Darren found the implicit expectation to give as director became overwhelming.

"Eventually I found I just couldn't keep up and would be spending hundreds, often on people I didn't know at all," he says.

As a middle ground, he decided to sign cards and only give money if he'd had direct contact. This stopped him feeling disingenuous and giving resentfully.

But the card-not-cash compromise has become harder as collections move online, with amounts often shown alongside the names of individuals by default.

Of course, these days, alongside emails, there's always the ever-present work WhatsApp group.

Healthcare worker Jeffrey says he's still reeling from seeing staff donations toward the family of a deceased patient being openly listed in the agency chat, individual donation amounts included.

Should you chase contributions - and note who's given and who has not?

"I send one email to those who haven't paid, making clear that those who have contributed are not included in the email. You'd be surprised how quickly people reply," she says.

She then gets a more junior colleague to send another, final, chaser on her behalf.

"And yes, I keep a list on paper, too. I don't forget," she adds.

"I don't like to nag," he says. Instead he prefers a single reminder to all that preserves team unity.

Thomas Roulet, professor of organisational psychology and leadership at Cambridge University, says:

Prioritise direct colleagues and close relationships: It's generally socially acceptable to limit giving toward wider team members

Do not chase people individually: And do not chase them collectively more than once. Some may be financially struggling

Include a card as an alternative: It costs the contributor nothing and feels like a souvenir for the recipient

The gift should be symbolic: Choose a gift for its individual significance rather than monetary value.

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, news. Trump: “Chiederemo a Europa soldi delle armi date da Biden a Kiev”
items.summary: Putin: “I contatti con Kiev continuano. Dialogo con Usa funziona”. Il Cremlino: “Non avvieremo un declassamento relazioni diplomatiche con Berlino”. Ma Lavrov avverte: “Chiuderemo le sedi del Goethe-Institut”. A Monaco ordigni esplosivi contro un’azienda della difesa, arrestati due cittadini bulgari: “Possibile attentato”. Gli 007 della Danimarca: “Mosca pronta a sabotare nostre industrie”
items.content:
Il presidente russo parla al Forum economico orientale di Vladivostok. Dopo l’arresto di due uomini sospettati di essere gli autori dell’attentato a Lipsia, e della conferma da parte del cancelliere tedesco Merz di una pista russa dietro quell’attacco, Lavrov avverte: “Chiuderemo le sedi del Goethe-Insititut” . Una misura in risposta alla chiusura di Casa Russa a Berlino ma il Cremlino non arriva allo strappo totale con la Germania. Peskov: “Non avvieremo un declassamento delle relazioni diplomatiche”.

Intanto, cresce in Europa l’allerta per sabotaggi e il rischio di attacchi ibridi russi (gli 007 danesi: “Mosca ha nel mirino le nostre industrie”).

Trump: “Chiederemo all’Europa e alla Nato i soldi delle armi date da Biden alla Ucraina”

Putin: “Un’ulteriore mobilitazione militare non è necessaria”

Putin: “Ci aspettiamo la piena ripresa delle relazioni con gli Usa”

Putin: “La minaccia di Kiev ai voli civili complica le possibilità di negoziati di pace”

Putin: “I contatti con Kiev continuano. Il dialogo con gli Usa sta funzionando”

A Monaco ordigni esplosivi contro un'azienda della difesa, due arresti

Cremlino: “Non avvieremo un declassamento delle relazioni diplomatiche con Berlino”

La ministra degli Esteri lettone: “Espansione verso Est della Nato un falso pretesto di propaganda russa”

Il governo lituano ha approvato oggi un progetto che prevede la fortificazione di alcuni complessi ospedalieri delle città di Vilnius e Kaunas, trasformandoli in centri strategici per la fornitura di servizi sanitari in caso di emergenza bellica o di altro genere. Commentando la decisione, il primo ministro lituano, Mindaugas Sinkevicius, ha affermato che la fortificazione di complessi ospedalieri seguirà modelli analoghi già operativi in Ucraina e in Israele e dei cui esperti la Lituania si avvarrà per la realizzazione dell'opera. Calcoli preventivi indicano che il costo complessivo dei lavori di fortificazione dovrebbe aggirarsi sui 300 milioni di euro.

Medvedev: “Germania ha intrapreso strada dell’oblio dei risultati della Seconda guerra mondiale”

Il vicepresidente del Consiglio di Sicurezza russo Dmitry Medvedev ha messo in guardia la Germania da una possibile escalation nei rapporti con Mosca, esortando Berlino ad adottare una linea più equilibrata nei confronti della Russia. "Mi sembra che debbano ravvedersi e adottare una linea molto più equilibrata, invece di cercare di entrare direttamente in uno scontro con il nostro Paese", ha dichiarato Medvedev, citato da Interfax. Secondo l'ex presidente russo, il cancelliere tedesco Friedrich Merz e alcuni esponenti del suo governo avrebbero intrapreso "la strada dell'oblio dei risultati della Seconda guerra mondiale", nonostante fino a poco tempo fa, a suo dire, la posizione di Berlino fosse diversa. "L'attuale cancelliere federale e i suoi collaboratori, di fatto, stanno portando avanti la triste opera dei loro predecessori", ha aggiunto Medvedev.

Sparatoria tra Servizi a Kiev, Zelensky licenzia i vicecapi delle due agenzie

Gli inviati americani Jared Kushner e Steve Witkoff "saranno a Kiev nei prossimi giorni" per riprendere i negoziati. Lo ha reso noto il presidente ucraino, Volodymyr Zelensky.

Norvegia sequestra una nave russa alle isole Svalbard. Mosca: “La rilasci”

Le autorità norvegesi hanno sequestrato alle isole Svalbard la nave russa Professor Molchanov, su richiesta del gruppo energetico statale ucraino Naftogaz, che punta a ottenere dalla Russia un risarcimento per i beni confiscati dopo l'annessione della Crimea nel 2014. Il sequestro, eseguito ieri dal governatore dell'arcipelago artico sulla base di un'ordinanza giudiziaria del 31 agosto, è stato disposto nell'ambito della richiesta di Naftogaz di ottenere da Mosca 4,22 miliardi di dollari. Nel 2023 un tribunale arbitrale dell'Aja si era pronunciato a favore della società ucraina, con una decisione riconosciuta dalla Norvegia. La Professor Molchanov, una nave da ricerca utilizzata principalmente per crociere di spedizione, è ora bloccata al molo di Barentsburg, insediamento minerario russo delle Svalbard. La nave resterà ferma in attesa di una nuova decisione del governatore o dei tribunali norvegesi.

Trump: “Chiederemo all’Europa e alla Nato i soldi delle armi date da Biden alla Ucraina”

Il presidente americano, Donald Trump , ha annunciato che chiederà agli europei e alla Nato di pagare le armi che l'amministrazione di Joe Biden aveva fornito gratuitamente all'Ucraina. "Vi prego di far sapere che l'amministrazione Biden ha fornito all'Ucraina molte più munizioni, senza alcun costo per loro, di quante ne abbiamo utilizzate in Iran. Centinaia di miliardi di dollari sono stati dati gratuitamente all'Ucraina e alla Nato, soldi che l'Europa avrebbe pagato - se solo glielo avessimo chiesto, ma chiederemo quei soldi, anche se con un certo ritardo! Grazie per l'attenzione che ci dedicherete", ha scritto il capo della Casa Bianca su Truth.

For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take… pic.twitter.com/0qtRMM7njo

Storica visita a Kiev del ministro degli esteri indiano: focus sulla Mar Nero e la sicurezza alimentare

La navigazione nel Mar Nero e la sicurezza alimentare. Sono due dei temi che saranno sul tavolo in occasione della storica visita a Kiev del ministro degli Esteri indiano Subrahmanyam Jaishankar. La visita di oggi di Jaishankar arriva dopo l'incontro tra il primo ministro indiano Narendra Modi e il presidente russo Vladimir Putin all'inizio della settimana. "Siamo grati all'India per il suo impegno a porre fine a questa guerra ingiusta", ha commentato sui social il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky dopo aver incontrato Jaishankar. "Abbiamo discusso della situazione nel Mar Nero, comprese le minacce esistenti alla navigazione civile", ha affermato Zelensky. "Ogni giorno in più di conflitto significa soltanto altre morti e altra distruzione", ha sottolineato il ministro degli Esteri indiano. "Comprensibilmente, spetta alle parti coinvolte trovare una soluzione. Ma se l'India può essere d'aiuto in qualsiasi modo, siamo pronti. E questo è stato finora l'obiettivo delle mie discussioni di oggi", ha aggiunto. Il ministro degli Esteri ucraino Andrij Sybiha ha definito la visita di Jaishankar un "momento storico". "Mentre il ministro era qui con noi a Kiev, la Russia ha lanciato ancora una volta gli 'Shahed' a propulsione a getto, sviluppati non senza l'aiuto dell'Iran", ha sottolineato Zelensky aggiungendo che la delegazione indiana "è rimasta al sicuro perché sono i caccia ucraini ad abbattere la maggior parte di questi droni". Dalla scorsa settimana, droni a propulsione a getto stanno attaccando Kiev e le aree circostanti, provocando molteplici allerte aeree ogni giorno, danneggiando edifici residenziali e causando vittime.

Mosca alla Germania: “Risposta appropriata a ogni escalation”

La Russia ha respinto categoricamente le accuse britanniche su un presunto coinvolgimento di Mosca nell'incidente con droni all'aeroporto di Lipsia e annunciato che risponderà in modo appropriata a ogni escalation dai Paesi europei. Lo ha riferito l'ambasciata russa nel Regno Unito dopo la convocazione dell'incaricato d'affari Vasily Tsyganov al Foreign Office. "Il 3 settembre, l'incaricato d'affari Vasily Tsyganov è stato convocato al ministero degli Esteri britannico, dove gli è stata consegnata una protesta nella quale si afferma il coinvolgimento della Russia nell'incidente con droni all'aeroporto di Lipsia", si legge in una nota della rappresentanza diplomatica. "Queste accuse infondate e assurde, formulate in uno stile britannico sorprendentemente familiare, sono state categoricamente respinte. Non è stata presentata alcuna prova convincente a sostegno della versione antirussa degli eventi", ha aggiunto l'ambasciata. La rappresentanza diplomatica ha sottolineato che Mosca "non cerca il confronto con il Regno Unito o con altri Stati europei". Tuttavia, ha avvertito, "qualsiasi passo volto all'escalation da parte loro riceverà una risposta appropriata e attentamente calibrata". (AGI)Bra

Il processo relativo agli attentati ai gasdotti Nord Stream dovrebbe iniziare il 14 ottobre presso la Corte d'appello anseatica di Amburgo. Il tribunale ha ammesso l'accusa contro il cittadino ucraino Serhij K. al processo di merito, ha comunicato una portavoce del tribunale. Lo riporta la Dpa. "In base a una valutazione preliminare dei fatti, la Sezione per la sicurezza dello Stato è giunta alla conclusione che, alla luce dei risultati dell'istruttoria, l'imputato risulti sufficientemente sospettato, in qualità di complice, del crimine di guerra consistente nell'uso di metodi di guerra proibiti mediante attacchi contro obiettivi civili, nell'innesco di un'esplosione con esplosivo, nella distruzione di opere edilizie e nell'interruzione di servizi pubblici", ha aggiunto la portavoce.

items.summary: Da giorni viene screditata dagli inviati del programma e da Sigfrido Ranucci, che avrebbe dovuto sostituire insieme a Daniele Piervincenzi
items.content:
La giornalista Giulia Presutti ha rinunciato alla conduzione del programma di inchieste Report al posto di Sigfrido Ranucci, rimosso dalla Rai lo scorso 28 agosto: per sostituirlo la Rai aveva scelto Presutti e Daniele Piervincenzi, anche lui giornalista investigativo.

Nei giorni successivi sia la redazione di Report che lo stesso Ranucci avevano fatto di tutto per screditarli. Subito dopo la loro nomina, Ranucci li aveva descritti come «due persone che mortificano le professionalità» di Report e del servizio pubblico e aveva definito «mediocre» la scelta di affidare a loro la conduzione del programma.

Presutti ha 36 anni, cominciò a collaborare con Report nel 2017 e ci ha lavorato fino all’ultima stagione, a parte una pausa di circa un anno che in questi giorni le è stata rinfacciata da Ranucci. Ha comunicato la sua decisione in una mail al direttore dei programmi di approfondimento della Rai Paolo Corsini.

Gli ha scritto: «In un contesto così complesso e delicato come quello che si è venuto a creare, faccio volentieri un passo indietro, nella speranza di aiutare in questo modo la trasmissione che mi ha formata e alla quale ho avuto l’onore di contribuire». Presutti ha aggiunto: «Una trasmissione così amata, che tanto ha dato al pubblico e alla nostra azienda, non può impantanarsi in discussioni e scambi così piccoli, né credo che il suo futuro possa essere legato a singoli nomi e singole personalità».

Ranucci aveva continuato a screditare Presutti e Piervincenzi anche nei giorni successivi alla loro nomina: in un post su Facebook aveva commentato un’intervista di Piervincenzi e rincarato le critiche verso entrambi: aveva rinfacciato loro alcuni favori, li aveva tacciati di ingratitudine, li aveva accusati indirettamente di essere stati «calati dall’alto» e, paragonando la propria carriera alla loro, aveva alluso al fatto che la loro esperienza non li renderebbe meritevoli della conduzione del programma.

Negli ultimi giorni Presutti, così come Piervincenzi, era stata oggetto di diversi articoli del quotidiano Domani che hanno sollevato questioni su di lei , e che avevano come fonti giornalisti di Report . Il gruppo degli inviati di Report in ogni caso aveva detto pubblicamente di non ritenere adeguata la scelta dei nuovi conduttori.

La Rai non ha dato spiegazioni ufficiali per la rimozione di Ranucci, ma si sa che il motivo ha a che fare con quanto emerso nelle indagini sull’attentato contro lo stesso Ranucci, compiuto a ottobre del 2025 e organizzato da Valter Lavitola , imprenditore coinvolto in diversi scandali della politica italiana degli ultimi vent’anni e molto amico di Ranucci.

Ranucci non è indagato, ma nell’inchiesta è emerso che aveva un rapporto molto stretto con Lavitola, che oltre a essere suo amico era anche una sua fonte, e con cui condivideva con disinvoltura molte informazioni sul suo lavoro. Il Comitato etico della Rai aveva condotto un’indagine interna analizzando chat, mail e audio recuperati dai dispositivi di Lavitola: tra le conversazioni ce n’erano alcune in cui Ranucci condivideva con Lavitola documenti interni della Rai, e altre in cui screditava pesantemente l’azienda.

Ranucci e la dirigenza della Rai avevano un rapporto conflittuale da tempo, a prescindere dall’attentato e dall’inchiesta, e anche per questo lo stesso Ranucci ha sostenuto che l’azienda stesse solo cercando un pretesto per farlo fuori.

items.title: 20 persone sono state arrestate in una vasta inchiesta sul caporalato in Calabria
items.content:
18 cittadini pakistani, uno bangladese e uno indiano sono stati arrestati in un’inchiesta della Direzione distrettuale antimafia di Catanzaro sul caporalato nella piana di Sibari, in Calabria, dove il primo giugno scorso quattro braccianti erano stati bruciati vivi in un minivan, secondo la procura dai caporali che li stavano riportando a casa dopo il lavoro. Le 20 persone arrestate nella nuova inchiesta sono indagate per associazione a delinquere finalizzata all’intermediazione illecita e allo sfruttamento del lavoro – in estrema sintesi, per caporalato –, e poi per estorsione e favoreggiamento dell’immigrazione clandestina. Tra i reati contestati c’è anche la riduzione in schiavitù.

Secondo l’indagine, i lavoratori sarebbero stati costretti a coabitare, fino a 20 persone contemporaneamente, in alloggi fatiscenti e privi di riscaldamento, luce e gas nei centri storici dei comuni della zona. Sempre secondo quanto emerso nell’indagine, ogni mattina sarebbero stati stipati in auto, minivan e furgoni e portati a lavorare in aziende agricole intestate a prestanome delle cosche mafiose.

Nell’indagine è emerso che gli imprenditori avrebbero pagato stipendi di 40 euro in nero per dieci ore di lavoro e direttamente ai caporali, che secondo l’accusa avrebbero trattenuto 5 euro al giorno per il trasporto e 60 euro al mese per l’affitto delle case in cui vivevano i braccianti. Le paghe non sarebbero state quindi versate regolarmente ai braccianti, che secondo l’accusa sarebbero stati ricattati con la minaccia di cacciarli di casa o con aggressioni fisiche. Sono informazioni coerenti con quello che aveva ricostruito il Post a giugno in alcuni approfondimenti sullo sfruttamento dei migranti in quella zona.

items.title: Le mostre del weekend, dagli Impressionisti a Henri Beaufour e Chiara Calore
items.summary: Nelle Marche la prima mostra in Italia dell'artista franco-siriano Fares Cachoux
items.content:
Dall'esperienza della scuola di Barbizon al dialogo tra Henri Beaufour e Chiara Calore, dalla riflessione sul corpo dei protagonisti della nuova figurazione internazionale alla prima personale in Italia dell'artista franco-siriano Fares Cachoux: sono alcuni degli appuntamenti di questa prima settimana di settembre.

PESCARA - Si intitola "La Scuola di Barbizon: le radici dell'Impressionismo" la mostra in programma dal 5 settembre al 9 gennaio al Museo dell'Ottocento Fondazione Di Persio-Pallotta che offre una lettura ricca e articolata dell'esperienza barbizonnais e dei suoi protagonisti, un gruppo di pittori che appunto iniziò a riunirsi nel villaggio di Barbizon, ai margini della foresta di Fontainebleau. Esposti per la prima volta insieme 120 dipinti (di Théodore Rousseau, Jules Dupré, Constant Troyon, Rosa Bonheur, Charles-François Daubigny e Narcisse Virgilio Diaz de la Peña, oltre a due opere di Gustave Courbet) della collezione della Fondazione, recentemente ampliata con nuove acquisizioni, che raccontano la pluralità dei linguaggi sviluppati all'interno della Scuola di Barbizon.

PADOVA - Diciassette tra i più autorevoli protagonisti della nuova figurazione internazionale (Radu Belcin, Enrica Berselli, Luca Bidoli, Greta Bisandola, Angelo Brugnera, Chiara Calore, Fabbio Copercini, Chandra Fanti, Angelo Giordano, Alfio Giurato, Maurizio L'Altrella, Julio Larraz, Nunzio Paci, Flavia Pitiș, Stefano Reolon, Nicola Samorì, Markus Schinwald) sono protagonisti alla Galleria Civica Cavour con la mostra "Sul futuro del corpo", a cura di Barbara Codogno, in programma dal 5 settembre al 4 ottobre. Attraverso oltre 50 opere, alcune di grandi dimensioni, gli artisti riflettono sul corpo, riportandolo alla sua dimensione più concreta ed enigmatica, come luogo dell'identità e della memoria.

VENEZIA - A Palazzetto Tito, sede della Fondazione Bevilacqua La Masa, dal 5 al 27 settembre arriva la mostra bi-personale "Tutte le creature abitano il confine", che si configura come una profonda conversazione visiva e concettuale tra Henri Beaufour e Chiara Calore. Il percorso espositivo guida il pubblico attraverso un continuo confronto tra opposti: eppure, nella diversità dei loro linguaggi, i due artisti sono accomunati da un'instabilità di fondo dei soggetti indagati, in bilico tra umano/animale, terreno/ultraterreno, quotidiano/mitologico.

GENOVA - Dal 4 settembre in mostra a Palazzo Ducale a Genova un'installazione multicanale su logistica marittima e crisi climatica dal titolo "Ninety Percent of Everything", realizzata dai collettivi Fish Tank e Fathom 30° insieme alla data artist Tiziana Alocci e alla factory sonora Stellare, con il contributo del fotografo Simone Lezzi. Il progetto installativo, in mostra fino al 4 ottobre e a cura di Maria Pina Usai, nasce in seguito alla call internazionale di U-Boot Lab volta alla selezione di artiste e artisti per una residenza di due settimane svoltasi tra Palazzo Ducale a Genova, il porto operativo, la stazione sperimentale del Cnr-Ias e in navigazione a bordo della nave cargo Grendi.

FAENZA (RA) - Dal 1° settembre all'11 ottobre Palazzo Milzetti - Museo Nazionale dell'età neoclassica in Romagna ospita "Presenze", una mostra personale di Alessandro Roma promossa in collaborazione con il Museo Internazionale delle Ceramiche di Faenza, organizzata in occasione di Argillà Italia 2026, Festival internazionale della ceramica. A cura di Domenico Iaracà, la mostra trova il proprio filo conduttore nella natura: in un dialogo con i dipinti murali, gli stucchi e le decorazioni del museo, le opere di Roma sembrano riappropriarsi di spazi che, solo in apparenza, sono privi dell'elemento naturale, dando vita a paesaggi interiori nei quali esperienze reali e immaginazione si incontrano.

CIVITANOVA MARCHE (MC) - Prosegue fino al 3 novembre presso lo Spazio Multimediale San Francesco "...Oltre", la prima mostra in Italia di Fares Cachoux, artista franco-siriano che utilizza l'arte come strumento di riflessione sulle questioni più urgenti del nostro tempo: politica, società e ambiente. Il progetto, a cura di Cristina Falco ed Enrico Lattanzi, è organizzato dal Museo Magma e da Cartacanta Aps e presenta le più importanti serie dell'artista caratterizzate uno stile minimalista dove colori vibranti e linee nette sono protagonisti.

Un viaggio tra musica, autodeterminazione e una dura lotta contro la depressione che passa anche attraverso i benefici dello sport: MP, da sempre appassionato di arti marziali, ha trovato nel pugilato un modo per stare bene. Abbiamo incontrato il rapper di Brebbia all’evento organizzato al Super Studio di Milano per il lancio di “Le cose cambiano”, il suo terzo disco, uscito l'1 dicembre, a due anni di distanza da “Solo tutto” certificato doppi
